merger_description:
Acquisition

This notification concerns the proposed acquisition of certain Australian assets of Konvoy Holdings Pty Limited (Receivers and Managers Appointed) (Subject to Deed of Company Arrangement) (**Konvoy**) by Kegstar Pty Limited (**Kegstar**), a wholly owned subsidiary of MicroStar Logistics, LLC (**Acquisition**).

The Australian assets which are proposed to be acquired pursuant to the Acquisition include:

(a) kegs;

(b) keg tracking technology hardware and software (known as 'Katch');

(c) select employees; and

(d) a keg repair and maintenance facility.

The Parties

MicroStar Logistics, LLC, is a limited liability company incorporated in the United States and is indirectly wholly owned by MStar Holding Corporation. MicroStar entered the Australian market in 2021 via the acquisition of Kegstar from Brambles.

In Australia, Kegstar primarily offers a pay-per-fill keg management service (PPF). It also offers longer-term keg leasing.

Konvoy operates a keg services business in Australia and New Zealand. It offers short-term keg leasing (on a PPF basis), longer-term keg leasing, and keg maintenance and repair services.

Summary of horizontal and vertical overlaps

The Parties are both suppliers of PPF services and, to a much lesser extent, longer term keg leasing to brewery customers in Australia.

There is no vertical overlap between the parties.

determination_table_content.details: | MicroStar Logistics – Kegstar (MN-30003) MicroStar Logistics – Konvoy MN-30003 This document contains a summary of the ACCC’s reasons for its determination of 7 August 2026. This document does not constitute the statement of the ACCC’s reasons for making the determination pursuant to sections 51ABZE(4)(b) and 51ABZZI(1)(b) of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth). The statement of the ACCC’s reasons will be published separately following a review for confidential information. Summary of Reasons 1. On 17 June 2025, Kegstar Pty Limited (Kegstar), sought informal clearance from the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) to acquire certain Australian assets of Konvoy Holdings Pty Limited (Receivers and Managers Appointed) (Subject to Deed of Company Arrangement) (Konvoy) (together, the Parties). On 23 October 2025, the ACCC announced that it opposed the acquisition. 2. Following the ACCC’s opposition, the Parties elected to seek clearance for the acquisition under Australia's new merger regime. On 6 February 2026, Kegstar lodged a notification with the ACCC in respect of Kegstar’s proposed acquisition of certain Australian assets of Konvoy (the Acquisition). The effective notification date was 20 February 2026.1 3. On 1 April 2026, the ACCC decided the Acquisition would be subject to a Phase 2 review and subsequently issued a Notice of Competition Concerns to Kegstar on 13 May 2026.2 The ACCC published a summary of the Notice of Competition Concerns on the Acquisitions Register on 14 May 2026.3 4. The ACCC has determined that the Acquisition must not be put into effect. A summary of the ACCC’s reasons for its determination is set out below. 1 [Redacted - confidential]. 2 ACCC, Phase 2 Decision, 1 April 2026, 72969.001.016.0500; ACCC, Notice of Competition Concerns, 13 May 2026. 72969.001.075.0001. 3 ACCC, Notice of Competition Concerns – Summary, 13 May 2026. 72969.001.037.0269. 1

| MicroStar Logistics – Kegstar (MN-30003) Keg pooling in Australia 5. Brewers use keg pooling services to facilitate distribution of kegged alcoholic beverages to licensed venues without needing to own, maintain or recover their own keg fleet. In Australia, brewers acquire keg pooling services from one of two providers – Kegstar or Konvoy. In summary: ▪ Kegstar introduced keg pooling services into Australia in 2012, when it commenced its keg pooling business. ▪ Konvoy entered the market in 2019 and rapidly emerged as a direct competitor to Kegstar, with competition between the Parties manifesting through active rivalry for customers and improved pricing, service offerings and commercial terms. ▪ Following a period of successful operation, Konvoy sought to expand into the United Kingdom and made investments in the development of a keg tracking technology platform. It then started experiencing increasing financial difficulties from 2024. ▪ Konvoy unsuccessfully sought additional capital and its secured lender declined to provide further funding in 2025. In March 2025, Konvoy entered administration and the secured lender appointed Messrs Crawford and Smith of McGrathNicol as Receivers. ▪ The Receivers conducted a sale process across March and April 2025 in which [Redacted - confidential].4 ▪ The Parties entered into an Asset Sale Agreement on 20 June 2025,5 which, if completed, would result in Kegstar becoming the sole provider of keg pooling services in Australia. The ACCC’s statutory task 6. The ACCC recognises that participants in a receivers’ sale process may pursue different objectives. Receivers are required to maximise returns for creditors (and the company), and the purchase price is clearly a key factor in maximising those returns. However, execution risk is also a relevant consideration. Where a sale process results in a firm seeking to acquire its closest competitor – which can carry with it the highest purchase price – significant competition concerns are likely to arise. 7. The ACCC’s role is not to determine the most efficient ownership structure for an industry, nor is it to assist receivers in obtaining the highest return for creditors. Rather, as an administrative decision-maker under Part IVA of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (the Act), the ACCC’s task is to assess the likely competitive effects of an acquisition in accordance with the statutory test. Under this regime, if the ACCC is satisfied that an acquisition, if put into effect, would, in all the circumstances, have the effect, or be likely to have the effect of substantially lessening competition in any market, it may determine that the acquisition must not be put into effect. The ACCC’s assessment in this matter is directed to that statutory question. 4 [Redacted - confidential]. 5 [Redacted - confidential]. 2

| MicroStar Logistics – Kegstar (MN-30003) Competitive effects of the Acquisition 8. The ACCC has assessed the likely competitive effects of the Acquisition in the market for the supply of keg pooling services in Australia. While brewers have alternative methods of distributing beverages to licensed venues, including cans, bottles and self- supplied kegs, the ACCC considers that keg pooling services constitute a distinct and valued service offering, and therefore a relevant ‘market’. For many brewers, particularly small and medium-sized brewers seeking to distribute products beyond their local area, keg pooling avoids the capital investment, logistical and administrative costs, and risks associated with self-supply of kegs. 9. The ACCC has assessed the Acquisition and has made the following findings based on the evidence before it: ▪ Kegstar and Konvoy are each other’s closest competitor. The evidence before the ACCC indicates that Konvoy’s entry led to vigorous head-to-head competition between the Parties, which is still continuing, including substantial price reductions, improved commercial terms and active rivalry for customers. ▪ If the Acquisition proceeds, Konvoy would cease to operate as an independent competitive constraint and Kegstar would become the sole provider of keg pooling services in Australia. The Acquisition would remove the only significant source of direct rivalry in the market. The ACCC considers that the loss of this head-to-head competition would be likely to reduce competitive pressure on Kegstar in relation to price, service quality, and commercial offerings to brewers. ▪ Absent the Acquisition, there is a real prospect that either an alternative purchaser would acquire Konvoy’s business as a going concern through a rapid and targeted sale process, or that a substantial proportion of Konvoy’s assets would otherwise be realised and deployed in competing keg pooling operations. ▪ Self-supply (following the Acquisition) would be unlikely to be sufficient to replace the competitive constraint currently imposed by Konvoy. While some larger brewers self-supply kegs and others may have the ability to do so for limited volumes or local distribution, the ACCC considers that a substantial portion of customers would be unlikely to switch to self-supply due to the significant capital investment, operational capability and ongoing logistical management required. ▪ Timely and sufficient new entry is unlikely. Although kegs and other key inputs are generally available, a new entrant would need to establish the operational capability, reputation and customer base sufficient to compete effectively. Konvoy’s management possessed a strong reputation and operational capability when it entered in 2019. However in the ACCC's view, the current limited availability of contestable customer contracts, likely customer consolidation following the Acquisition, and the challenges of achieving scale make timely and effective new entry unlikely. 10. Having regard to the matters outlined above, the ACCC considers that competition in the future with the Acquisition would likely be substantially less than in the future without the Acquisition. 11. The ACCC does not consider that the Proposed Undertaking offered by Kegstar addresses the extent of the competitive harm arising from the Acquisition. That harm is substantial and arises from a significant structural change in the market to a monopoly provider of keg pooling services in Australia. The ACCC considers that a behavioural and 3

| MicroStar Logistics – Kegstar (MN-30003) time-limited remedy would not sufficiently replicate the structural competitive constraint provided by an independent competitor. 12. For these reasons, the ACCC is satisfied that the Acquisition, if put into effect, would, in all the circumstances, be likely to have the effect of substantially lessening competition in the Australian keg pooling services market and has determined that the Acquisition must not be put into effect. 4

Background The acquirer – Kegstar 2.1. Kegstar is a wholly owned subsidiary of MicroStar Logistics, LLC (MicroStar), which is a limited liability company incorporated in the United States. MicroStar is an independent keg services company that has operations in the United Kingdom, Europe, Australia and New Zealand. It entered the Australian market in 2021 via acquisition of the Kegstar business from Brambles. 2.2. Kegstar provides keg pooling services to brewers of a range of sizes. Its largest customers in Australia by number of fills in 2025 included: [Redacted - confidential].6 It also supplies a range of small to medium brewers. 6 [Redacted - confidential]. 5

| MicroStar Logistics – Kegstar (MN-30003) 2.3. Kegstar primarily offers keg pooling services in Australia. Keg pooling services are explained at 2.11 to 2.13 below. It also offers longer-term keg leasing. Kegstar had approximately [Redacted - confidential] keg fills in 2025.7 The target – Konvoy 2.4. Konvoy operates a keg services business in Australia and New Zealand. It offers keg pooling services, longer-term keg leasing, and keg maintenance and repair services. 2.5. Konvoy provides keg pooling service to brewers of a range of sizes. Its largest customers in Australia by number of fills in 2025 included: [Redacted - confidential].8 It also supplies many smaller brewers. Konvoy had approximately [Redacted - confidential] keg fills in Australia in 2025.9 2.6. Further information on keg pooling services, including their supply in Australia, is set out below. Overview of keg pooling services 2.7. In Australia, beer and cider are mostly sold through two major channels, being: ▪ ‘on-premise’, which includes the sale of ‘kegged alcoholic beverages’ (served through taps) and ‘packaged alcoholic beverages’ (in bottles and cans) for consumption in licensed venues, and ▪ ‘retail’ where ‘packaged alcoholic beverages’ are sold in retail outlets. 2.8. A typical keg is made from stainless steel, has a capacity of 50L, can be stacked for easy storage, and is reusable. While kegs can come in other sizes and be made from materials other than stainless steel, the ACCC understands that those kegs usually serve specific uses. For example, alcoholic beverage producers may use single-use plastic kegs when exporting alcoholic beverages as the kegs do not need to be returned and are typically cheaper.10 2.9. Producers of alcoholic beverages (typically brewers) who wish to have their drinks served on tap in licensed venues will fill empty kegs and then arrange for them to be delivered to licensed venues. Once a stainless-steel keg has been emptied at the venue, the keg must then be collected. 2.10. The beverage producer can use its own kegs and arrange for delivery and collection or can use a keg pooling service. 2.11. Keg pooling (sometimes known as ‘pay-per-fill’, or PPF) is a service in which a provider owns a pool of kegs and supplies empty kegs to customers (which are primarily brewers), using either its own vehicles or third-party logistics providers. Figure 1 below shows how keg pooling differs from self-supply. 7 [Redacted - confidential]. 8 [Redacted - confidential]. 9 [Redacted - confidential]. 10 The usage of plastic kegs is considered in further detail at paragraph 6.10 below. 6

| MicroStar Logistics – Kegstar (MN-30003) 2.12. With keg pooling, customers clean and refill the kegs and generally use their preferred logistics provider to transport filled kegs to licensed venues (known as ‘forward logistics’). 2.13. Once the keg(s) have been emptied at the venue, the keg pooling service provider then organises the pick-up of empty kegs (known as ‘reverse logistics’). These kegs may be stored at a warehouse if required or otherwise delivered directly to customers (not necessarily the customer that last used the keg) for the cycle to repeat. Customers pay for this service based on the number of times they fill these kegs. Figure 1: Keg pooling (blue) compared to self-supply (red) Source: [Redacted - confidential]. Keg pooling services in Australia 2.14. Keg pooling services were introduced in Australia in December 2012 by Kegstar. Kegstar was founded by Adam Trippe-Smith.11 At that time, the only option for brewers seeking to sell their product on tap was to own or lease kegs and coordinate logistics internally or outsource this function to logistics providers.12 Kegstar’s model was attractive to brewers and by 2013 there were some customers relying solely on Kegstar for their keg needs.13 11 [Redacted - confidential]; Brambles, Media Release, Brambles Acquires 100% of Kegstar: Kegstar commences rapid global expansion, 1 December 2015. 72969.001.073.0001. 12 [Redacted - confidential]. 13 [Redacted - confidential]. 7

| MicroStar Logistics – Kegstar (MN-30003) 2.15. In 2014, the global supply-chain logistics company Brambles became a 30% shareholder in Kegstar.14 Brambles provided Kegstar financial support, supply-chain expertise and access to its global network.15 2.16. By the end of 2015, Kegstar had a pool of 50,000 kegs across three countries – Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom, with plans to expand into mainland Europe.16 At that time, Brambles acquired 100% of the Kegstar business from Adam Trippe-Smith and co-shareholder Shane Bradley.17 2.17. In 2017, Kegstar acquired Keg Lease Pty Ltd, a specialist keg leasing company focused on the Australian craft beer industry operating under the Bintani brand, from the Meddings family. [Redacted - confidential].28 While initially signalling its support, AquAsia wrote to Konvoy on 5 March 2025 to advise that additional funding would not be provided.29 3. Kegstar’s Notification and the assessment process Notification lodgement and timeline 3.1. Kegstar voluntarily notified the Acquisition on 6 February 2026. In accordance with section 51ABY of the Act, on 13 February 2026, the ACCC decided that the notification submitted on 6 February 2026 should be taken to not have an effective notification date because it was materially incomplete. On 20 February 2026, MicroStar provided additional information and documents in response to the ACCC’s decision under section 51ABY of the Act. Accordingly, the effective notification date is 20 February 2026.30 3.2. On 1 April 2026, the ACCC decided the notification would be subject to Phase 2 review and published its decision to this effect. On 13 May 2026, the ACCC provided its Notice of Competition Concerns (NOCC) for this matter to Kegstar. On 14 May 2026, the ACCC published a summary of the NOCC on the Acquisitions Register. 3.3. The ACCC is required to make its determination in relation to the Acquisition by 17 August 2026. Market engagement and information gathering 3.4. Over the course of its assessment, the ACCC has engaged with, and received substantial submissions and information from Kegstar, Konvoy and its Receivers, McGrathNicol, the senior secured creditor, AquAsia, and customers and other interested parties. 3.5. In doing so, the ACCC gathered information on both a voluntary and compulsory basis, including: ▪ sending voluntary requests for information and documents; ▪ issuing compulsory notices seeking the provision of information and production of documents under sections 155(1)(a) and (b) of the Act; ▪ conducting voluntary interviews; and ▪ conducting compulsory examinations of individuals under section 155(1)(c) of the Act. 3.6. Australia’s new formal mandatory and suspensory merger control regime came into effect on 1 January 2026. The acquisition provisions in this regime apply to acquisitions of shares or assets of a corporation, as well as other types of legal rights.44 4.2. Businesses that propose to give effect to an acquisition that meets the notification thresholds must notify it to the ACCC.45 Businesses may also voluntarily notify an acquisition to the ACCC. Section 50 of the Act, which prohibits the acquisition of shares or assets that have the effect, or likely effect, of substantially lessening competition in any market, does not apply to notified acquisitions. 4.3. Kegstar voluntarily notified the Acquisition to the ACCC. 4.4. The ACCC is the administrative decision maker under the new formal merger regime and determines whether a notified acquisition may be put into effect or must not be put into effect.46 A proposed acquisition that is required to be notified or has been notified is stayed until the ACCC or Australian Competition Tribunal determines that it may be put into effect.47 Substantial lessening of competition test 4.5. The ACCC may determine that a proposed acquisition must not be put into effect only if it is satisfied that the acquisition, if put into effect, would, in all the circumstances, have the effect, or be likely to have the effect, of substantially lessening competition in any market.48 The concept of lessening competition includes preventing or hindering competition.49 4.6. The substantially lessening of competition test (SLC test) requires a focus on whether the effect or likely effect on competition of a proposed acquisition is substantial. This has been interpreted to mean an effect that is real or of substance, and therefore meaningful and relevant to the competitive process.50 4.7. In the context of mergers, the SLC test is a forward-looking test that ‘requires a comparison between the nature and extent of competition in the future with the acquisition and without the acquisition in any market potentially affected by the acquisition.’51 4.8. As is the case in this assessment, the ACCC recognises that there may be a number of possible future scenarios absent an acquisition. The ACCC’s starting point for delineating relevant markets is to identify the products and geographic regions actually or potentially supplied by the merger parties and focusing on the overlaps between the products or geographic regions supplied by the merger parties. The ACCC then considers if any other products and geographic regions constitute relevant close substitutes. 6.3. The ACCC uses a framework called the Hypothetical Monopolist Test to assess whether substitutes are sufficiently close to be included in the relevant market. The relevant question is whether a hypothetical current and future profit-maximising monopolist could effectively exercise market power by profitably imposing a small but significant and non-transitory increase in price (SSNIP) over the focal product (or group of products) and geographic area. If a hypothetical monopolist supplier of this product cannot profitably institute a SSNIP because customers would switch to alternative products in sufficient quantity to render the price increase unprofitable, the next closest demand substitute is added. The collection of products and/or geographies is expanded until a hypothetical monopolist supplier could profitably institute a SSNIP over the focal product(s). 6.4. Customer option to purchase kegs 9.27. The Proposed Undertaking contains an obligation on Kegstar to offer customers the option to purchase kegs from Kegstar at market value upon termination or expiration of the customer’s contract. 9.28. Kegstar submitted that this addresses countervailing power concerns by providing a practical, cost-effective pathway for customers to transition to self-supply or to another provider without needing to purchase new kegs at full price. It is said to eliminate the capital cost barrier as an impediment to self-supply, by allowing customers to acquire kegs at book value rather than replacement cost.343 9.29. While the option to obtain kegs at a lower price would be a more attractive alternative than purchasing kegs at full price, brewers nevertheless need funding or capital to purchase kegs. Further, the other main impediment for brewers seeking to self-supply is the operational capability and ongoing logistical management to organise and oversee the reverse logistics of returning the kegs. These factors are not addressed by the Proposed Undertaking. The ACCC does not consider that this obligation, even in conjunction with the rest of the Proposed Undertaking, would result in a sufficient proportion of brewers being able to credibly switch to self-supply so as to remedy the loss of an independent competitive constraint. Service level commitments with termination rights 9.30. The Proposed Undertaking provides customers the right to terminate their contracts with Kegstar without penalty if Kegstar materially fails to meet certain KPIs and does not remedy the failure within a reasonable period. Those KPIs cover on-time delivery of empty kegs, timely collection of empty kegs from venues, turnaround time to re-perform keg services, supplier review meetings, billing accuracy and customer support response times. 9.31. Kegstar submitted that this addresses the risk that Kegstar could degrade service quality by providing customers with an enforceable exit right, and practical protection against any diminution in service standards for a period of time and time to plan to change to an alternative keg logistics solution without penalty.344 9.32. While such a right could possibly limit competitive harm in respect of service quality, ultimately, the ACCC considers the effect is likely to be very limited in circumstances where market feedback indicates customers do not have an alternative keg pooling service provider to switch to and self-supply is not an option for a material 343 [Redacted - confidential]. 344 [Redacted - confidential]. 56

| MicroStar Logistics – Kegstar (MN-30003) portion of customers.345 Such a time-limited obligation does not provide the same competitive constraint on Kegstar’s ability to reduce quality of service as an independent competitor would. 9.33. Accordingly, based on the evidence before it, the ACCC does not consider that the Proposed Undertaking addresses the significant competitive harm arising from the Acquisition. While some specific obligations in the Proposed Undertaking have the potential to improve some conditions for competition, the time-limited, behavioural obligations do not adequately address the longer-term competitive harm arising from a significant structural shift to a monopoly keg pooling service provider brought about by the Acquisition. 10. Conclusion 10.1. The ACCC is satisfied that the Acquisition, if put into effect, would, in all the circumstances, be likely to have the effect of substantially lessening competition in the supply of keg pooling services in Australia. 10.2. The ACCC has considered both the state of competition with the Acquisition and absent the Acquisition. With the Acquisition, Konvoy’s assets would be acquired by Kegstar and Konvoy would cease to competitively constrain Kegstar. This would leave Kegstar without a direct competitor. Without the Acquisition, while there is a possibility that Konvoy and its assets may permanently exit the market, there remains a real commercial prospect of Konvoy’s business being acquired as a going concern through an alternate sale process, or a substantial portion of its assets being acquired and deployed in keg pooling services. 10.3. The ACCC does not consider that self-supply would sufficiently competitively constrain Kegstar in the future with the Acquisition. While some larger brewers may be able to switch entirely to self-supply, the ACCC considers that a substantial portion of customers would be unable to switch significant volumes to self-supply due to the costs, operational capability and logistics required to self-supply. 10.4. The ACCC also does not consider that timely and sufficient entry would be likely. A new entrant may be able to secure kegs and logistics services, but would be unlikely to be able to attract a sufficiently large customer base in a timely manner to compete effectively. 10.5.
